summary.text: Falcon 9 is a partially reusable, two-stage medium-lift rocket designed and built in the United States by SpaceX.
Its booster can land vertically so it can be flown again, first achieved in December 2015, and individual boosters have flown as many as 37 times.
In 2020 it became the first commercial rocket to launch humans to orbit, and it has seen the most launches among active launch vehicles.

items.prompt: A Falcon 9 booster lands upright after finishing its job. What is that for?

options.label: To slow the payload before it reaches orbit
To let the second stage drop its cargo more gently
To make it possible to fly the same booster again
To bring the crew back to the launch site

items.explain: The booster is capable of landing vertically to facilitate reuse.

items.prompt: On a Falcon 9 flight, what is the second stage's job?

options.label: To speed the payload up to its target orbit
To lift the whole rocket off the launch pad
To land upright so that it can be reused
To carry the booster up to a set altitude

items.explain: The first stage carries the second stage and payload to a predetermined speed and altitude, after which the second stage accelerates the payload to its target orbit.

items.prompt: How did the funding of Falcon 9 differ from SpaceX's earlier Falcon 1?

options.label: Falcon 9 was paid for entirely by NASA, unlike Falcon 1
Falcon 1 had NASA flight purchases arranged and Falcon 9 had none
Neither one had any customers arranged before it was built
Falcon 9 also used private capital, but NASA had committed to buy flights

items.explain: SpaceX paid for Falcon 1 itself with no pre-arranged sales, while Falcon 9 was also built with private capital but with NASA commitments to buy flights once capabilities were shown.

items.prompt: A 2011 NASA report compared building a Falcon 9-class rocket the traditional way with a more commercial approach. What did it find?

options.label: The two ways would have cost about the same
The traditional way would have cost far more: about US$4 billion against a possible US$1.7 billion
The commercial way would have cost more, since firms add profit
The traditional way would have cost far less, since NASA reuses designs

items.explain: The report estimated about US$4 billion under NASA's traditional contracting, while a more commercial approach might have let the agency pay only US$1.7 billion.

items.prompt: After a launch, the two halves of the cover that protected the payload come back down. What happens to them?

options.label: They burn up on the way down
They land upright on legs, as the booster does
They parachute down, are scooped from the water, and can fly again
They are left behind in space

items.explain: The fairing halves are scooped out of water after a parachute-assisted landing and can be reflown multiple times.

items.prompt: What does NASA's "Category 3" listing of Falcon 9 let the agency do?

options.label: Launch its most expensive, important and complex missions on it
Skip safety reviews on any mission that uses it
Fly crew only, and never cargo
Launch only low-cost test missions

items.explain: NASA lists Falcon 9 as a Category 3 (Low Risk) launch vehicle, which allows it to launch the agency's most expensive, important and complex missions.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Falcon 9 is a rocket designed and built in the United States by SpaceX. It has two stages, is partly reusable, and is classed as a medium-lift launcher. The first stage, called the booster, lifts the second stage and the payload to a set speed and height; the second stage then carries the payload the rest of the way to its orbit. Both stages use SpaceX Merlin engines, burning very cold liquid oxygen with a rocket-grade kerosene called RP-1.

paragraphs.heading: Flying again
paragraphs.text: A key feature of Falcon 9 is reuse. The booster can come back and land upright so it can fly again, and this was first done on the 20th flight, in December 2015. By November 7, 2026, SpaceX had landed boosters 659 times, and single boosters have flown as many as 37 times. Even the fairing halves drift down under parachutes, are pulled out of the water, and can fly several more times.

paragraphs.heading: Its record
paragraphs.text: Falcon 9 first flew on June 4, 2010. It launched its first Commercial Resupply mission to the International Space Station on October 8, 2012, and in 2020 it became the first commercial rocket to send people to orbit. With 698 successful flights, it has launched more often than any other active rocket, with two failures in flight, one partial failure and one rocket destroyed before flight. In January 2021 a single Falcon 9 carried 143 satellites into orbit, a record for one rocket.

paragraphs.heading: Trusted with big jobs
paragraphs.text: Falcon 9 is rated to carry NASA astronauts to the space station and is certified for the US National Security Space Launch program. NASA's Launch Services Program places it in its low-risk category, which lets it launch the agency's most costly and complex missions. The rocket has gone through several versions, from v1.0 in 2010 to the Block 5 variant flying since May 2018.

paragraphs.heading: How it was paid for
paragraphs.text: SpaceX paid for its previous rocket, Falcon 1, with its own money. Falcon 9 was also built with private money, but NASA had agreed in advance to buy several flights once the rocket showed certain abilities. Under NASA's Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program, a deal first worth US$278 million, later raised to US$396 million, covered three demonstration launches carrying the Dragon cargo spacecraft. In 2008 SpaceX also won a US$1.6 billion contract for at least 12 missions carrying supplies to and from the space station.

paragraphs.heading: Cost and name
paragraphs.text: In 2011 SpaceX put the development cost of the first version at about US$300 million. NASA estimated the same work would have cost US$3.6 billion under a traditional cost-plus contract. The rocket's family name comes from the Millennium Falcon, the starship in the Star Wars films.
